hops.title: Hearing your own eyeballs move
hops.text: In 1998, Lloyd Minor and colleagues at Johns Hopkins described patients missing bone over the superior semicircular canal. That gap acts as a third mobile window, changing how sound and pressure travel through the inner ear; loud tones can make the room spin. Later work noted loud footsteps and audible eyeball movements, plus an exam finding: some patients hear a vibrating tuning fork on an ankle bone. Diagnosis requires characteristic symptoms, high-resolution CT showing the gap, a physiological sign such as a low cervical VEMP threshold (81 versus 98 dB nHL in affected and control ears in Minor's 2005 series), and no better vestibular explanation. Surgery can help.

sources.citation: Minor LB, Solomon D, Zinreich JS, Zee DS (1998). Sound- and/or pressure-induced vertigo due to bone dehiscence of the superior semicircular canal. Archives of Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery 124(3):249-258.
Ward BK, Carey JP, Minor LB (2017). Superior Canal Dehiscence Syndrome: Lessons from the First 20 Years. Frontiers in Neurology 8:177.
Minor LB (2005). Clinical manifestations of superior semicircular canal dehiscence. The Laryngoscope 115(10):1717-1727.

Ward BK, van de Berg R, van Rompaey V, Bisdorff A, Hullar TE, Welgampola MS, Carey JP (2021). Superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome: Diagnostic criteria consensus document of the committee for the classification of vestibular disorders of the Bárány Society. Journal of Vestibular Research 31(3):131-141.

hops.title: Why the driver rarely gets carsick
hops.text: Explanations for why the driver rarely gets carsick often point to the road view, head movements or knowing what is coming. In 1991, Arnon Rolnick and Robert Lubow tested control on its own. Across 22 pairs of volunteers exposed to identical nauseating rotation, they matched vision, head motion, activity and predictability, while one person in each pair controlled both the rotation and the paired head movements. Controllers reported significantly fewer symptoms than their passive partners. Charles Oman and Kathleen Cullen later proposed that persistent activity in vestibular neurons signaling a mismatch between expected and actual motion feedback might help trigger nausea through an unidentified brainstem mechanism.

sources.citation: Rolnick A, Lubow RE (1991). Why is the driver rarely motion sick? The role of controllability in motion sickness. Ergonomics 34(7):867-879.
Oman CM, Cullen KE (2014). Brainstem processing of vestibular sensory exafference: implications for motion sickness etiology. Experimental Brain Research 232(8):2483-2492.
Roy JE, Cullen KE (2004). Dissociating self-generated from passively applied head motion: neural mechanisms in the vestibular nuclei. The Journal of Neuroscience 24(9):2102-2111.

hops.title: Twenty-seven days in left-right reversing prisms
hops.text: In a 1976 study, four volunteers at McGill University wore head-mounted prisms that reversed their vision left to right for 2, 6, 7 and 27 days. With the view reversed, the normal VOR made the image slide farther with each side-to-side turn. Within a week, the VOR gain of the longer-wearing volunteers fell to roughly a quarter of normal. In dark tests, the 27-day volunteer's reflex lagged normal by 130 degrees, close to the 180 of a full reversal, and regained half its usual gain. After the prisms came off, timing was near normal within two hours; gain took two to three more weeks.

sources.citation: Gonshor A, Jones GM (1976). Extreme vestibulo-ocular adaptation induced by prolonged optical reversal of vision. The Journal of Physiology 256(2):381-414.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Head-mounted reversing prism goggles rest on a wooden lab bench beside a mirror reflecting a coffee mug.
image.caption: After 27 days in left-right reversing prisms, one volunteer's horizontal eye reflex shifted toward reversal at half normal gain.
